module_title: Elastic Load Balancing, Routing and Target Health
review_basis: Individually visually inspected original SAP Module 08 slides 13–15.
part_title: NLB Transport, TLS, Zonal Addresses and Flow Health

scenes.title: NLB transport and TLS listener behavior
scenes.visual_overview: The first panel lists TCP, TLS, UDP, TCP_UDP and supported QUIC-related listeners with restrictions. The second compares TLS termination at an NLB with encrypted passthrough over TCP port 443. The third lists instance, eligible private IP and ALB targets, while the fourth warns against unqualified throughput promises.
visual_walkthrough: Compare NLB Layer 4 listener choices including configuration restrictions
Follow client TLS to the TLS listener's certificate and contrast TCP pass-through to the backend
Inspect supported instance, private-IP and ALB targets and compatible listener and target protocols
Explain that performance and connection limits depend on actual workload and configuration
scenes.visual_example: A financial service requiring end-to-end TLS termination at the application chooses a TCP listener on port 443 rather than letting a TLS listener terminate the session.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Choose the termination point and transport protocol first, then verify eligible targets and performance.
scenes.narration: This slide asks us to design the Network Load Balancer from the transport layer upward. Begin at the upper-left diagram with listener options. TCP, TLS, UDP and combined TCP and UDP serve different flow patterns; the slide also lists supported QUIC-related options subject to their configuration restrictions. These are not application-layer HTTP routing rules. Move to the upper-right side and follow the encrypted connection. A TLS listener terminates the client's TLS session at the NLB and needs a compatible certificate. By contrast, a TCP listener on port four four three can pass encrypted TLS bytes through, so the backend application terminates the connection. The distinction determines where the security boundary actually lies. Below, compare instance targets, private IP targets from eligible address ranges, and an Application Load Balancer as a target. Public IP targets are not supported, and placing an ALB behind NLB requires a compatible TCP target group. The final panel warns against treating marketing-style latency or unlimited capacity claims as architectural guarantees. Check practical flow counts, routing, TLS termination, monitoring and target capacity. The correct exam design starts with transport and TLS behavior, then checks target compatibility.

scenes.title: NLB addresses, DNS and original client identity
scenes.visual_overview: Three upper panels depict static zonal IPs, regional versus zonal DNS names, and Proxy Protocol v2 metadata. A lower traffic path separates DNS-based NLB node choice from cross-zone target selection.
visual_walkthrough: Inspect one static zonal address per enabled NLB Availability Zone and optional Elastic IP assignment for internet-facing IPv4
Distinguish regional healthy-node DNS answers from a single zonal DNS endpoint
Explain client source-IP preservation dependence on protocol and target settings and optional Proxy Protocol v2
Trace client-to-node DNS selection separately from node-to-target cross-zone balancing
scenes.visual_example: A client allowlist uses each enabled NLB zonal Elastic IP and keeps more than one zonal address to avoid a single-zone dependency.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Zonal address stability does not ensure resilience; clients and targets must tolerate zone failures.
scenes.narration: The central theme is that a Network Load Balancer has a zonal address model. Start on the left with three Availability Zones, each showing a stable NLB address. An internet-facing IPv4 configuration can assign an Elastic IP per enabled zone, useful for customer allowlists. But pinning all clients to one zonal address creates a zone dependency. In the middle panel, follow regional DNS responses to healthy NLB nodes across zones. A zonal DNS name resolves to one specific zone's load-balancer node, so the calling application needs its own availability plan when it chooses a zone directly. Next, inspect the rightmost client-identity panel. Whether the backend sees the original client IP depends on the transport protocol, target type and configuration. Proxy Protocol version two can carry connection metadata to a compatible application, but sending that header to an application that cannot parse it can break traffic. Finally, follow the lower picture from client DNS toward the NLB node, then from that node toward targets. DNS and zonal affinity influence the first selection; cross-zone balancing influences the second. They are different mechanisms and should be tested separately.

scenes.title: NLB flows, health checks and fail-open behavior
scenes.visual_overview: The upper-left shows colored persistent flows assigned to particular targets. The upper-right shows TCP, HTTP or HTTPS health probes. The bottom illustrates failed-zone DNS updates and connection timeout or target failure.
visual_walkthrough: Trace a connection's flow-based target assignment and ongoing affinity
Select TCP, HTTP or HTTPS probes; for UDP traffic use a representative supported non-UDP health check
Inspect zonal health-driven DNS changes and possible fail-open when all targets are unhealthy or a group is empty
Explain TCP connection continuity, idle timeout, target termination and why healthy new capacity does not migrate an old connection
scenes.visual_example: An online game uses UDP transport yet serves a TCP or HTTP readiness probe that accurately reflects the UDP service's health.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A load balancer chooses transport flows and healthy targets; it does not migrate every in-progress connection.
scenes.narration: This slide separates the lifetime of a connection from the health of a server. Begin at the upper-left. NLB uses flow characteristics, including protocol and endpoint addresses and ports, to select a target. Once the flow is established, packets in that flow stay with the selected target under normal conditions. Now examine the health-check panel. Active checks support TCP, HTTP or HTTPS. A UDP-only service therefore needs an appropriate non-UDP health endpoint whose result honestly represents the UDP application's readiness. In the lower-left, failed zonal target capacity can cause unhealthy zonal NLB addresses to disappear from DNS answers. But that does not mean a universally enforced traffic block. If all eligible targets are unhealthy, the NLB can fail open, and empty target groups introduce their own failure behavior. Finally, the lower-right panel shows why connection management matters. Idle timeout, termination and unhealthy-target configuration can affect an existing flow. Adding new healthy targets does not transparently move the state of a live TCP session onto a different server. Test both connection establishment and ongoing sessions during target and zone failure.
